source.title: Scaling Laws for Neural Machine Translation
source.authors: B. Ghorbani; O. Firat; Markus Freitag; Ankur Bapna; M. Krikun; Xavier García; Ciprian Chelba; Colin Cherry

record.file_problem: None; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures scaling in encoder-decoder NMT and argues that a single law based only on total parameters is insufficient: loss depends on encoder/decoder allocation and data composition. It refines the scope and form of scaling claims.
record.gate_note: The reported results concern cross-entropy scaling, out-of-sample prediction, parameter allocation, data composition, and translation quality. The paper also cites findings from other work; those cited results are not recorded as rows. Figure trends are included only when the text explicitly describes them.
record.test_reason: The study fits power laws to held-out cross-entropy of encoder-decoder NMT models from about 40M to 3B parameters. It argues that a univariate law in total parameters fails, while a bivariate encoder/decoder law fits and predicts held-out runs. It also shows that scaling depends on test and training data composition. Its own results bear on V2, V4, V5, V6 and V7 in a new training regime (supervised translation). It does not test LM pretraining (V1) or compute-optimal allocation (V3).
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that NMT scaling is predictable with a bivariate encoder/decoder law, but a total-parameter law is insufficient, and the exact form may vary by architecture or task. They find that scaling exponents and the loss–quality link depend heavily on whether test sets are source- or target-original. With back-translated training data, test loss stops improving and then worsens beyond about 400M parameters; forward-translated data lets even small models reach very low training-subset loss. They raise concerns about synthetic web text.
record.recipe_differences: Measures held-out cross-entropy while scaling model parameters, but studies conditional encoder-decoder NMT rather than decoder-only language models; varies encoder and decoder capacity separately and proposes a bivariate law.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome varies with encoder-versus-decoder scaling, source- versus target-original evaluation composition, training-data construction, language pair, and translation-quality metric. Width and internal layer configuration are held fixed.

fits_no_version.finding: Proposition 1 gives the loss-minimising split of a fixed parameter budget between encoder and decoder, in proportion to the fitted exponents.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In encoder-decoder models, the optimal encoder/decoder parameter split follows the ratio of component scaling exponents.

record.problems: The main architecture sweep varies depth while holding width and other internal settings fixed. The proposed law is fit to the study's own runs; the out-of-sample test changes scaling strategy but is not orders-of-magnitude extrapolation. Composition-specific conclusions are tied to the tested translation datasets. Beam-search settings were not tuned for each model, and the authors note possible effects of search strategy on quality comparisons.
record.rows_left_out: No separate row for every domain/test set or every model size: the paper reports many such curves and fit statistics in Figures 12–16, but the rows above retain the explicitly described aggregate findings and representative Web Domain 1 results. Training-data composition results are represented by the stated aggregate trends and the approximately 0.16 training-subset loss; no separate values were recoverable from the plots in the text.

untested.parts: Entire version: the study trains no language models, only supervised encoder-decoder NMT. Token and compute scaling are also not varied.
Extrapolation over orders of magnitude: the held-out runs extend under 2x beyond the fit range.
Entire version: there is no parameter/token split under a compute budget.
Width, heads and other internal dimensions are held fixed. Only depth and the encoder/decoder split vary.
Image/video, repeated data, fine-tuning and transfer are not tested. Data-size scaling in NMT is also not tested.
Sensitivity to fitting method, parameter-counting convention or training schedule is not tested, and the original sources' laws are not compared.

missing.what: Source-original and target-original test sets have drastically different fitted exponents. The authors contrast this with LM results, where test sets only changed constants.
missing.locator: Section 3, 'The Effect of Test Set Construction', Figure 5

missing.what: The additive test-loss penalty for lopsided Nd/N allocations at 5×10^8 parameters is plotted per test set. Only qualitative text is given ('much worse multiplicative constant').

record.verdict_notes: V1 links were removed throughout, because the models are supervised NMT systems rather than pretrained language models; these rows bear on V5. V4 and V2 verdicts treat the architecture and extrapolation findings as applicable beyond LMs. The extrapolation distance is modest (under 2x). Fits use soft_l1 robust regression with f_scale picked from a grid; sensitivity to this choice is not reported. The study is not one of the original sources.

versions.untested_parts: Tests parameter scaling in encoder-decoder NMT, not token-count or compute scaling, nor language models where parameters, tokens, and compute are independently varied.
Tests extrapolation from encoder/decoder scaling runs to symmetric NMT runs within the reported model range; not extrapolation to runs orders of magnitude larger.
Does not optimize parameter and token counts under a fixed compute budget. Its encoder/decoder allocation result is a different allocation problem.
Varies depth and encoder/decoder allocation while holding internal layer width and other configuration fixed; does not broadly vary width or other architectural details.
Tests conditional text generation for NMT and synthetic/back-translated training data. Does not test image/video, repeated-data training, fine-tuning, or transfer.
Tests BLEU and BLEURT relationships with cross-entropy on translation test sets, not predictability across other downstream task families.

Shows dependence on architecture, evaluation/training data composition, and language/task setting. It does not compare alternative fitting procedures to establish sensitivity to fitting method, or directly test disagreements between the original sources.

labels.reason: Encoder and decoder exponents differ, evaluation composition changes exponents, and back-translated training data produces a reversal beyond roughly 400M parameters.

relation.reason: Its own scaling experiments and fitted laws directly test several claim versions.

tranche.reason: The study shows that total-parameter scaling needs an encoder/decoder qualification, synthetic training data can reverse test-loss improvements, and generation quality can deteriorate despite improving cross-entropy.

source_check.notes: Figure 7 thresholds and Figure 6 allocation penalties are fitted-law estimates. The supplied text identifies itself as a preprint under review and mentions an initial NeurIPS 2021 submission; it does not substantiate the pack's ICLR 2021 reviewed designation.

statements.correction: Encoder-decoder NMT; total-parameter-only law insufficient; bivariate encoder/decoder law fits; approximately 2.2 billion back-translated training examples; test loss deteriorates beyond roughly 400M parameters; no fine-tuning/transfer formula tested.
statements.problem: The NMT findings are accurate, but their framing as evidence about fine-tuning or transfer is unsupported: these experiments train NMT models rather than testing a pretraining-to-fine-tuning transfer formula.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The total-parameter univariate fit is inadequate, while the bivariate encoder/decoder fit is accurate; token and compute scaling are not tested (r1–r4).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: English→German symmetric scaling runs held out from fitting
reader_labels.reason: The law fitted on encoder/decoder runs predicts symmetric-run losses with R² 99.8 in the reported Web Domain 1 conditions (r5–r6).

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Encoder versus decoder scaling and allocation
reader_labels.reason: Encoder and decoder exponents differ, and encoder-scaled models can yield better translation quality at similar loss; the paper reports architecture allocation is consequential rather than uniformly slight (r1–r2, r8–r9, r19).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Conditional text translation and synthetic-data training
reader_labels.reason: A bivariate law works across the tested NMT settings, but total parameter count alone fails, and synthetic-data training can show test-loss reversal or early low-loss behavior (r3–r8, r12–r14).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: BLEU and BLEURT improve as cross-entropy falls on target-original sets (r15, r17).

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.reason: Cross-entropy improves while BLEU deteriorates beyond a threshold, and BLEURT mirrors this breakdown (r16, r18).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Architecture allocation and evaluation/training data composition
reader_labels.reason: The results show different encoder/decoder exponents, failure of a univariate total-size fit, composition-dependent scaling, and test-loss deterioration for large models trained on back-translated data (r1–r2, r8–r13).
